newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street seen sharply higher at open.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street seen sharply higher at open.

text.p: Wall Street stocks were seen rising sharply at the open on Tuesday, recovering from comments by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, which created fears about a possible Japanese disposal of U.S. Treasuries and sparked a sell-off in stock markets yesterday.
But the stock market, which was also battered Monday by profit-taking and sell programs, could then settle down and might even see more declines, analysts said.
"We should get a snap-back at the start," Larry Wachtel, an analyst at Prudential Securities, said.
"That's normal after a viscious shake-up like we had yesterday," Wachtel said. "But it's not necessarily up, up and away from there. We could see the market settle down again."
U.S. stocks trading in London were already starting to recover, as the Japanese Finance Ministry acted to defuse the impact of Hashimoto's comments by saying he had been incorrectly reported.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average registered its second-largest point decline ever on Monday, finishing down 192.25 points to 7604.26.

Stocks reeled after Hashimoto, responding to a question following a speech at Columbia University in New York, was quoted as saying Japan in the past had been tempted to sell U.S. government bonds holdings and boost its gold reserves but had not done so.

But Japan moved to calm markets, saying Hashimoto had been incorrectly reported. Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said on Tuesday: "The prime minister's real intention was not correctly reported."
A senior finance ministry said American government bonds were an essential investment tool in Japan's foreign reserves.

"The market is likely to respond to the overnight calming moves by Japan," Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock & Co said. "It has better perspective on the remarks made by the Japanese Prime Minister and we could see some bargain hunting this morning."
Thom Brown, managing director of Rutherford Brown and Catherwood, called yesterday's stock market decline an example of irrational panic and said it was caused by profit-taking.
In early trade, the Standard & Poor's 500 futures index was up 7.25 points at 889 and the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond rose 8/32 to a 6.69 percent yield.
Japan's Nikkei average closed off 94.21 points at 20,341.93.
In London, the FTSE 100 was up 14.2 points at 4590.
The dollar extended overnight losses against the yen but was off lows. It was trading at 114.35/40 yen in Tokyo and at around 1.7233/38 marks in Europe.

The Wall Street Journal said in its Heard on the Street column that Wall Street finds it hard to fathom that Tele-Communications Inc founder Bob Magness might have neglected to plan for death and taxes. But some tax-estate specialists say his estate's last tax bill may be much less than originally thought.
The New York Times said a potential rheumatoid arthritis drug could help boost the shares of Immunex Corp.
